title: On-call and incident response playbook
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Overview

This playbook defines Redwood's standard on-call and incident response practices. It covers incident classification, the life cycle from detection to postmortem, operational runbooks for high-priority services, rotation and escalation rules, game day planning, and customer-facing status page/communications templates. This document is intended for engineers, SREs, support, and product owners.

Scope

- Applies to all Redwood-hosted services and customer-facing control plane components.
- Includes Hosted API, Dedicated control plane endpoints, Console, and the Private control plane managed by Redwood.
- Does not replace customer-specific runbooks for on-prem clusters; reference the Private deployment docs where applicable.

Roles & Responsibilities

- Primary on-call (Tier 1): First responder for alerts and customer-impact incidents. Responsible for initial triage and mitigation.
- Secondary on-call (Tier 2): Technical escalation for issues that require deeper product/runtime knowledge.
- Incident Commander (IC): Coordinates response for Sev 1/Sev 2 incidents, owns comms and timeline.
- Postmortem Author: Produces the incident review and coordinates follow-ups.
- Service Owner: Approves mitigations and long-term remediation plans.
- Support/Customer Success: Crafts customer communications and assists with account-specific impact analysis.

Severity Definitions and SLOs

- Sev 1 (Critical): Service unavailable or major degradation for >5% of customers or critical control plane outage. Target MTTR: 60 minutes. Pager path: Primary on-call -> IC within 15 minutes.
- Sev 2 (High): Significant feature degradation impacting a cohort of customers with no immediate workaround. Target MTTR: 4 hours.
- Sev 3 (Medium): Partial impact or reduced performance with clear mitigation. Target MTTR: 24-72 hours.
- Sev 4 (Low): Non-urgent issues, bugs, or UX inconsistencies. Address in normal sprint planning.

SLOs and thresholds (examples):

| Metric | SLO | Alert threshold |
|---|---:|---:|
| API 99th p50 latency (text generation) | p50 < 150ms | p50 > 250ms for 5m |
| Error rate (5m window) | < 0.1% | > 0.5% sustain 5m |
| Control plane availability | 99.95% monthly | outage > 3m |

Incident Lifecycle (Procedural Steps)

1) Detection
   - Alerts originate from Prometheus/Alertmanager, synthetic tests, customer reports, or the status page monitoring.
   - Alerts must include runbook links, recent log snippets, and affected regions/services.
2) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   - Primary on-call acknowledges the alert in PagerDuty within 5 minutes.
   - Determine scope: affected service(s), customer impact, regions, and whether a workaround exists.
   - Set severity (Sev 1-4) and notify stakeholders.
3) Engage (15-30 minutes)
   - For Sev 1/2 open an incident channel (Slack #incident-[short-id]) and assign an IC.
   - IC runs the incident timeline and coordinates cross-team engagement.
4) Mitigate and stabilize
   - Follow service-specific runbooks (see Runbooks section).
   - If mitigation requires short-term config changes, document the change in the channel and record rollback steps.
5) Recovery
   - Confirm full recovery with production checks and synthetic tests.
   - Keep customers and internal stakeholders informed of status and ETA.
6) Post-incident (RCA)
   - Within 24 hours: IC publishes an initial incident summary and timeline in the incident channel.
   - Within 72 hours: Postmortem draft created by Postmortem Author.
   - Within 7 days: Final postmortem published, action items assigned with owners and due dates.

Severity Decision Checklist

- Number of affected customers > 10%? => Sev 1 or 2.
- Control plane degraded for management tasks? => at least Sev 2.
- No known workaround and critical SLA exposed? => escalate severity.

Runbooks (Operational Playbooks)

Each critical service must have a one-page runbook accessible from alert metadata. Runbooks must include: owner, primary/secondary contacts, quick diagnostics, common mitigations, safe rollback instructions, and key dashboards.

Minimum runbook template (one-page):
- Service name
- Owner and contacts
- Pager escalation path
- Symptoms -> likely causes -> quick checks (commands, dashboards)
- Immediate mitigations (with exact CLI/API commands)
- Revert steps and safety notes
- Related dashboards and logs

Example quick-checks (CLI)
- Check API node health:
  curl -sS https://api.redwood.example.com/health | jq
- Check sidecar logs (k8s):
  kubectl -n redwood logs -l app=api --tail=200
- Synthetic checks status: check synthetic-dashboard > "generation-requests"

Escalation and Rotation Policy

- Rotation length: 1 week for primary on-call, 1 week for secondary.
- Handoff process: outgoing on-call creates a Handoff note in the #oncall-handoffs channel summarizing outstanding incidents, ongoing mitigations, and known flakiness.
- Escalation timeline: Primary on-call must escalate to Secondary if issue unresolved after 30 minutes for Sev 1, 2 hours for Sev 2.
- On-call fatigue policy: rotations skip engineers with >2 consecutive rotations unless they opt-in. Replacements should be arranged with at least 48h notice.

Game Day Planning

Objectives: validate runbooks, test detection/alerting, exercise cross-team coordination, and improve tooling.

Game day checklist:
- Define scope and success criteria (e.g., recover from simulated control plane outage within 60 minutes).
- Create a non-production environment and synthetic traffic generator.
- Notify stakeholders and schedule a post-game-day retrospective.
- Simulate incident and time each step: detection, triage, mitigation, recovery.
- Capture learnings and convert to action items.

Postmortems and Blameless Reviews

- Every Sev 1 and Sev 2 must have a written postmortem. Sev 3/4 postmortems at discretion of Service Owner.
- Postmortem template (must be in the body of the postmortem page):
  1. Summary (1-2 sentences)
  2. Impact (customer / system impact and duration)
  3. Timeline (ordered events with timestamps)
  4. Root cause analysis (why the issue occurred)
  5. Immediate mitigation steps taken
  6. Long-term remediation (action items with owners and due dates)
  7. Preventative measures and follow-ups
  8. Lessons learned

- Reviews are blameless: focus on systems and process improvement.
- All postmortems must have at least one follow-up work item scheduled within 30 days.

Status Page and Customer Communications

Principles:
- Clear, factual, and timely.
- Use plain language and avoid internal jargon.
- Provide regular updates until resolved; note ETA when known.

Status page template fields:
- Incident ID
- Start time
- Services affected
- Geographic scope
- Current status (identified / investigating / monitoring / resolved)
- Customer impact description
- Mitigation steps taken
- Next update ETA

Sample short customer-facing updates:
- Initial: "We are investigating elevated error rates in the Redwood API affecting a subset of requests in us-west-2. Our engineering team is triaging; we will post an update within 30 minutes. Incident ID: INC-2026-042"
- Mitigation: "We identified a problematic autoscaling configuration impacting request routing. We have applied a fix and are monitoring traffic. Error rates are decreasing. ETA for full recovery: 30 minutes. Incident ID: INC-2026-042"
- Resolved: "The incident affecting text generation in us-west-2 is resolved. Root cause: misconfigured autoscaler policy causing scheduler thrash. Full recovery confirmed at 2026-02-15T14:12Z. If you continue to see issues, contact support@redwood.example.com. Incident ID: INC-2026-042"

Internal comms cadence for Sev 1/2:
- 0m: Pager triggered, channel created, IC assigned.
- 15m: Initial incident summary posted to leadership and Product.
- 30m: Customer-facing status page update posted.
- 60m: Check-in with execs on impact and mitigation plan.
- Post-resolution: 24h initial summary, 72h draft postmortem, 7d final review.

Metrics and Dashboards to Monitor During an Incident

- Error rate (per service, per region) 1m/5m windows.
- Request latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99).
- Queue/backlog length for async workers.
- Resource utilization (GPU memory, CPU, network).
- Autoscaler activity and pod restarts.

Communication Templates (Slack snippets)

- Create channel: "/incident create INC-[short] title: [short description]"
- Initial IC post: "IC: @name | Sev: [1/2/3] | Impact: [brief] | Current hypothesis: [short] | Action: [next step] | Owners requested: @[teams]"

Retention, Compliance, and Post-incident Data

- Incident channels and logs are retained per the security retention policy. Sensitive customer data must not be pasted into public channels.
- For incidents involving customer data exposure, notify Security and Compliance immediately and set confidentiality: restricted.

Runbook Ownership and Maintenance

- Service owners must review runbooks quarterly and after any Sev 1/2 incident.
- Runbook checklist for owner review:
  - Links to dashboards still valid
  - Contact list up-to-date
  - Command snippets tested in a staging environment
  - Playbook includes rollback steps and safety checks

Appendices

A. Quick escalation phone list (example)
- On-call pager: +1-555-0101 (PagerDuty)
- Eng-SRE lead: +1-555-0102 (Marco Alvarez)

B. Incident tagging taxonomy
- Tag incidents by: service, region, root_cause_category (deploy, infra, config, external), customer_impact_level.

C. Common runbook snippets
- Roll back config map:
  kubectl -n redwood rollout undo deploy/api --to-revision=3
- Drain node for maintenance:
  kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

D. Post-incident follow-up tracker (recommended columns for the actions table)
- Action ID | Short description | Owner | Due date | Status | Link

E. Suggested drill cadence
- Monthly micro-drills (15-30 minutes) focused on a single runbook.
- Quarterly full game-days (2-4 hours) with cross-team participation.
